traveler: Charles Ponzi (Carlo Pietro Giovanni Guglielmo Tebaldo Ponzi)
title: The Coupon and the Line: Lugo to Boston to the Charity Ward
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Lugo, the five given names
stops.date_confidence: attested; birth date and place consistent across Wikipedia and Britannica. Flagged: some tertiary accounts give Parma as birthplace, which is where he was raised, not where he was born.
stops.campa: A son is born in Lugo, in the province of Ravenna, to Oreste Ponzi and Imelda Tommasini, and given five names: Carlo Pietro Giovanni Guglielmo Tebaldo. The Tommasini side keeps a memory of money it no longer has, and the boy grows up inside that memory rather than inside the money. The parish record marks nothing else about the day. Later accounts, copying one another, will move the birth ninety kilometres west to Parma, where he was only brought up. Lugo has put up no marker that would correct them, and none that names him at all.
suggested_refs: The town of Lugo, Ravenna, which has raised no monument, plaque, or marker to him
sources: wanderingitaly.com, 'Pilgrimage and Ponzi Schemes: Lugo, Italy' (firsthand visit finding no marker)

stops.name: Parma, the son of a fallen line
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Parma upbringing is Zuckoff's account as digested by Smithsonian and is the city Ponzi himself gave reporters. Date is an ordering placeholder within a childhood no source dates.
stops.campa: The family settles him in Parma, and Parma is the city he will give reporters for the rest of his life when they ask where he comes from. The household runs on the story of the Tommasini fortune: what it was, who lost it, and how a son might set about getting it back. Nothing in any record reached says the fortune was ever real. He learns the register of a class his parents no longer belong to anyway: the manners, and the assumption that money comes back to families who deserve it.
suggested_refs: Mitchell Zuckoff, Ponzi's Scheme: The True Story of a Financial Legend (2005), on the family's remembered prosperity
sources: Mary Darby / Mitchell Zuckoff, 'In Ponzi We Trust', Smithsonian Magazine

stops.name: Rome, the Sapienza and the spendthrift
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; attendance rests on Ponzi's own memoir and duration is disputed, one account giving about a year and others a longer dissipation. Pinned at Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza, the university's seat in his day; the Citta Universitaria was not built until 1935.
stops.campa: He is enrolled at the University of Rome, whose seat is then the Palazzo della Sapienza beside Piazza Navona, and he falls in with students richer than he is. He keeps up with them. He goes to the cafes and the theatres and pays his share, and the family money goes, and he leaves without a degree. It is the first time he spends money that is not his on the appearance of belonging to people who have it. By his own telling he does not regret the education. He never mentions what the family said.
stops.quote: In my college days, I was what you would call here a spendthrift.
stops.quote_source: Ponzi to the New York Times, as quoted in Mitchell Zuckoff, 'In Ponzi We Trust', Smithsonian Magazine
suggested_refs: The Palazzo della Sapienza complex and the church of Sant'Ivo, seat of the University of Rome until 1935
sources: Mass Humanities, on the memoir account

stops.name: Naples, boarding the Vancouver
stops.date_confidence: attested as to port, ship and month; the exact sailing date within November 1903 was not separately verified.
stops.campa: He boards the Dominion Line steamship Vancouver at Naples in November, bound for Boston by way of the Azores. He is twenty-one. He carries whatever the family can still put together for him, which is not much and is more than they can spare, and the passage is the last thing they buy him. What happens on board between Naples and the Azores exists only in the account he gives of it decades later, and nobody else aboard is ever named. The ship works out of the bay past Vesuvius into the winter Atlantic.
suggested_refs: Dominion Line passenger-list holdings for the SS Vancouver, 1903 season, GG Archives

stops.name: Ponta Delgada, the mid-ocean call
stops.date_confidence: the Azores call is attested through the line's schedule (GG Archives records the Vancouver's 1903 service as Naples to the Azores to Boston), not through a fetched passenger itinerary. The date is an ordering estimate inside the crossing. The shipboard card game is Ponzi's uncorroborated self-report.
stops.campa: The Vancouver calls at Ponta Delgada on Sao Miguel, the halfway mark of a route the line runs from Naples to the Azores to Boston. The line's schedule records the call, so the port is not in question. Somewhere on this crossing, by the story he tells afterward, a cardsharp takes almost everything he has, so that he steps ashore in America with two dollars and fifty cents. For the card game there is no witness but Ponzi, and he first tells it years later, when he is famous.
suggested_refs: The harbour of Ponta Delgada, Sao Miguel, scheduled Azores call of the Naples-Boston service
sources: GG Archives, Dominion Line passenger-list holdings

stops.name: Boston Harbor, the landing
stops.date_confidence: date, ship and city attested (Wikipedia; Smithsonian). The pier is a gap: no source reached names it, and Long Wharf is used only as the period's principal passenger landing point. The $2.50 is Ponzi's own accounting and is corroborated by nothing.
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of November the Vancouver ties up in Boston and Carlo Ponzi walks into the United States at twenty-one, with no English, no trade, and nobody waiting. The city takes in thousands like him that season, off a dozen lines a week, and keeps no separate record of this one. He will say afterward that he came off the ship with two dollars and fifty cents, and nothing corroborates the figure. The date and the ship are written down. The pier he steps onto is not.
stops.quote: I landed in this country with $2.50 in cash and $1 million in hopes, and those hopes never left me
stops.quote_source: Ponzi to the New York Times, as quoted in Mitchell Zuckoff, 'In Ponzi We Trust', Smithsonian Magazine
suggested_refs: Long Wharf, Boston, principal passenger landing of the period; the actual pier of the 1903 arrival is undocumented

stops.name: New York, the years with no employer's name
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; a generic pin for an itinerant period. No employer, address, or date for any job between 1903 and 1907 is documented in any source consulted. The date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: For four years he works whatever will hire a man with an accent and no papers worth showing: dishwasher, waiter, clerk, labourer, interpreter for other Italians who have less English than he does. He learns the language off the customers. This is the longest stretch of his life about which the record says nothing, and whatever anyone knows of it is known because he chose, later, to tell it. No employer's name survives, no address, no dates, no wage.
suggested_refs: The undocumented 1903-1907 itinerancy, reconstructed only from Ponzi's own later accounts

stops.name: Florida, the signs he could not paint
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no city or town is specified in any source found, so the coordinate is a state centroid placeholder. Date is an ordering estimate within 1903-1907.
stops.campa: He turns up in Florida and takes work painting signs, a trade he has never learned. The lettering goes badly. He can hold a job anywhere for a few weeks by convincing someone he can do the thing, and then cannot do the thing, and leaves before the work catches up with him. Twenty years on he will be back in this state under another name, selling ten-dollar lots cut out of a hundred acres of it, part of that swamp. Which town he paints in, no account says; the state is the whole of what anyone recorded.
suggested_refs: The unlocated Florida sign-painting episode, c. 1903-1907

stops.name: Banco Zarossi, the six percent
stops.date_confidence: attested as to bank, street, year, alias and mechanism (Wikipedia; Duhaime). Two corrections carried: the alias is Charles Bianchi, with no supported middle initial, and he entered as assistant teller or clerk, the rise to manager being Zuckoff's reconstruction rather than a documented appointment. Zarossi's flight to Mexico is reported consistently but is reconstruction, not court record.
stops.campa: In Montreal he calls himself Charles Bianchi and takes a clerk's stool at Banco Zarossi on Saint-Jacques Street, a bank for Italian immigrants run by Luigi Zarossi. It pays depositors six percent, twice what the other banks pay, and it pays them out of the money new depositors bring in that same week. Ponzi watches this work for months before it stops working. When the bank fails Zarossi is gone to Mexico with what is left, and Ponzi is standing in Montreal with no job, no money, and a complete education.
suggested_refs: Banco Zarossi, Saint-Jacques Street, Montreal, and its 6 percent deposit rate

stops.name: Saint-Vincent-de-Paul, inmate 6660
stops.date_confidence: conviction, sum, forged signature and inmate number attested. Coordinates corrected to the National Historic Site in Laval (Parks Canada; Wikidata Q23303428); an earlier working figure sat 4.5 km southwest on Montreal island. Term dated 1908-1910 rather than Wikipedia's 1908-1911, because the National Archives Atlanta file holds a 1910 mug shot and dates the federal term 1910-1912. The contradiction is flagged, not resolved.
stops.campa: He forges a check for four hundred and twenty-three dollars and fifty-eight cents on the Canadian Warehousing Company, copying the signature of a director named Damien Fournier, and is caught at once. The court sends him to the penitentiary at Saint-Vincent-de-Paul, north of the city on the Laval side of the river, where he is entered as inmate number 6660. The sum is recorded to the cent, the signature he copied has a name on it, and the register has the number. How long he serves is the one thing the sources cannot agree on.
suggested_refs: Saint-Vincent-de-Paul Penitentiary, Laval, National Historic Site of Canada
sources: Parks Canada / Canada's Historic Places listing
National Archives, Prologue, 'When Ponzi's Bubble Burst' (Summer 2010), for the incompatible 1910 date

stops.name: Atlanta, the file the Archives keep
stops.date_confidence: attested; National Archives Atlanta inmate case file, dating the confinement 1910-1912 and holding the 1910 mug shot. Coordinates corrected to 601 McDonough Blvd SE; an earlier working figure fell 3.5 km northeast in Cabbagetown.
stops.campa: Out of Canada, he is picked up helping five Italians cross the border into the United States without papers and drawn into a federal case. Two years at the penitentiary in Atlanta, and about a month more because he cannot pay the fine. The National Archives keeps the file: the mug shot, and the measurements a clerk takes of his ears and his forearms. He is twenty-eight. In eleven years a Boston newspaper will wire this prison to ask whether the warden remembers him, and the warden will.
suggested_refs: National Archives at Atlanta, inmate case file of Charles Ponzi, U.S. Penitentiary Atlanta, 1910-1912
sources: National Archives, Prologue, 'When Ponzi's Bubble Burst' (Summer 2010)

stops.name: Blocton, the skin off his own back
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the primary and effectively only source is Ponzi's own autobiography, chapter VII. The nurse's name is corrected to Pearl Gossett. The area of skin donated is given variously as 50, 122, and about 200 square inches, and is not resolved here. Coordinates correct for West Blocton, Bibb County.
stops.campa: At a mining camp in Bibb County he works as an interpreter and helps at the camp hospital. A gasoline stove explodes while a nurse named Pearl Gossett is cooking a patient's meal, and her left arm, her shoulder and part of her breast are burned to charred flesh. Grafts are needed and nobody volunteers. Ponzi gives skin off his own body, a large area of it, and spends months in a bed himself recovering. The only person who ever tells this story is Ponzi, in his own book, and the amount of skin grows in the telling.
suggested_refs: Charles Ponzi, The Rise of Mr. Ponzi, chapter VII, the Pearl Gossett grafts

segments.name: Boston, the Clerk and the Coupon

stops.name: Boston, the desk at J. R. Poole's
stops.date_confidence: employer and year attested (Smithsonian). Placement is reconstruction: the address of Poole's office is not attested in any source reached, and a working note that placed it on School Street conceded it could not be told apart from the later Niles Building address. Pinned separately from 27 School Street on purpose, so as not to imply a documented address.
stops.campa: He answers a newspaper advertisement from a Boston merchandise and export broker named J. R. Poole and is taken on as a clerk and stenographer. The qualification is his languages: he can write a business letter in Italian, French and English, and Poole trades overseas. For the first time since Parma he is a man with a desk. All day he reads the firm's foreign correspondence, the terms and the postage and the rates at which one country's money turns into another's. Where Poole's office stood is not written down anywhere reachable.
suggested_refs: J. R. Poole, Boston merchandise and export broker, employer of record in 1917; office address undocumented

stops.name: Somerville, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: date and place attested by genealogical record (WikiTree Gnecco-10, Middlesex County), month corroborated by Smithsonian. The church or civil venue within Somerville is not identified in any source found, so city-centre coordinates are a placeholder. The descriptor 'Boston-born' has been dropped: no source locates Rose's birthplace.
stops.campa: He meets Rose Maria Gnecco, a stenographer, and on the fourth of February they marry in Somerville. She is twenty-two. She does not know about Montreal or about Atlanta; she will learn both from a newspaper two and a half years from now. Rose stays with him through the bankruptcy, the indictments, three trials, the Florida land, the faked suicide and the arrest in New Orleans, and does not follow him onto the boat to Italy. She outlives him by forty-four years.
suggested_refs: Massachusetts marriage record, Somerville, Middlesex County, 4 February 1918

stops.name: Hanover Trust, the two thousand refused
stops.date_confidence: the refusal of a $2,000 loan by Hanover Trust in 1919 is attested (Wikipedia, 'Hanover Trust Company'). What the loan was for is contradicted: that source attaches it to the reply-coupon scheme, while the Trader's Guide framing is Zuckoff's reconstruction. Not resolved. Coordinate is an unconfirmed North End placeholder: no source located gives a street number for the bank.
stops.campa: He builds an international commercial directory, the Trader's Guide, a listing of firms in many countries to be paid for by the advertising carried in it, and takes the plan to Hanover Trust for a loan of two thousand dollars. The bank declines. He has no security and no history in Boston to stand in place of it, and the name means nothing to the men across the desk. No copy of the Guide has since been located, so what he showed across the desk that day cannot be examined. Within eighteen months he will own this bank, holding its stock and sitting on its board.
suggested_refs: Hanover Trust Company, Boston; the surviving copies of the Trader's Guide have not been located

stops.name: Boston, the coupon out of Spain
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the origin story is Ponzi's self-report as related by Smithsonian and is not independently documented. Pinned at a downtown Boston placeholder because no address for the correspondence is recorded.
stops.campa: A letter comes from a correspondent in Spain about the Trader's Guide, and inside it is an international reply coupon, the postal instrument that lets a sender prepay an answer from abroad. The coupon is bought in the currency of the country that issues it and redeemed in the country that receives it, and after the war those currencies no longer match. Bought cheap in Rome, cashed in Boston, one coupon can be worth several times what it cost. He does the arithmetic and the arithmetic works. The arithmetic is the only part that ever works.
suggested_refs: The international reply coupon under the Universal Postal Union convention, and the post-war currency spread that made the arbitrage arguable on paper

stops.name: 27 School Street, the certificate filed
stops.date_confidence: attested; In re Ponzi, 268 F. 997 (D. Mass. 1920), which also found the concern a one-man sole proprietorship and the Daniels advance a loan rather than a partnership investment. Coordinate note: two sources give 42.3585 and 42.3579 for this address, some 65 m apart; the former is used here.
stops.campa: On the day after Christmas he files a business certificate in Boston naming himself sole manager of the Securities Exchange Company, room in the Niles Building at 27 School Street. The seed is two hundred dollars from a furniture dealer named Joseph Daniels, which Daniels will later call a partnership and a federal referee will call a loan. He promises fifty percent in ninety days. In February he takes in about five thousand dollars. By June the figure is two and a half million.
suggested_refs: The Niles Building, 27 School Street, Boston (1915, Charles Howard Walker), still standing and unmarked
sources: aknextphase.com, 'The Niles Building: Hub of a Financial Scandal'

stops.name: 27 School Street, the partners who were not partners
stops.date_confidence: the filing date and the court's findings are attested in In re Ponzi, 268 F. 997; the characterisation of Bertollotti as probably already dead and of Dondero as an agent rather than a partner is the court's, reported as such.
stops.campa: With Fidelity Trust threatening to attach what he has, he files a second certificate naming two partners, John S. Dondero and Guglielmo Bertollotti. The federal court will find the partnership fictitious, got up to put the money behind names an attachment cannot reach. Dondero is ruled an agent and not a partner. The concern keeps no books worth the name and employs no accountant. Bertollotti, the court records, was in all likelihood already dead on the day his name was written down.
suggested_refs: In re Ponzi, 268 F. 997 (D. Mass. 1920), on the fictitious partnership and the Fidelity Trust attachment

stops.name: Lexington, 19 Slocum Road
stops.date_confidence: purchase terms and the roughly six-week occupancy are attested by real-estate journalism drawing on public records (Boston Globe, 2023). The month is an ordering estimate: sources give the summer of 1920 and the arrest in August.
stops.campa: He buys 19 Slocum Road in Lexington from an industrialist named Richard Engstrom for thirty-nine thousand dollars, on a condition Engstrom accepts: that Engstrom put money into the Securities Exchange Company. The seller finances the buyer by becoming his depositor. It is a Colonial Revival house on a wide lot, the sort of address the Tommasini money was supposed to have bought two generations back in Italy. Rose keeps house in it. They live there about six weeks.
suggested_refs: 19 Slocum Road, Lexington, Massachusetts, still standing and periodically on the market
sources: Boston Globe, 'Former Lexington home of Charles Ponzi on the market for $4.3 million' (2023)

stops.name: Suffolk County Courthouse, the two hundred dollars comes back
stops.date_confidence: attested that Daniels sued for $1 million and attached Ponzi's assets in July 1920; the precise day, given elsewhere as 2 July, could not be confirmed from any accessible docket and has been reduced to month precision. Pinned at the Suffolk County courthouse; the specific court in which the equity bill was entered is not itemised in the sources reached.
stops.campa: Joseph Daniels, the furniture dealer whose two hundred dollars started the thing seven months earlier, files in equity for an accounting of the profits and attaches Ponzi's property for one million dollars. It is the first hard number any court has put on him, and the papers print it everywhere. Depositors read it as proof that he is worth a million; the Commonwealth reads it as a reason to start asking questions. The federal referee will throw out the partnership theory, and Daniels recovers nothing.
suggested_refs: Daniels v. Ponzi, the July 1920 equity bill and $1,000,000 attachment, discussed in In re Ponzi, 268 F. 997

stops.name: Hanover Trust, the certificate for a million and a half
stops.date_confidence: attested by Cunningham v. Commissioner of Banks, 249 Mass. 401 (decided 5 June 1924): the fictitious 'Lucy Martelli' account and the $1,500,000 certificate dated 22 July 1920, later split into three of $500,000. A working claim that the accounts were opened 24 May 1920 is not in the opinion and has been dropped. Coordinate is an unconfirmed North End placeholder; no street number for the bank is given by any source located.
stops.campa: He is by now a director of Hanover Trust and its effective owner, having bought the stock with money handed across the counter at School Street by people who thought they were buying postal coupons. One of the accounts on the books is carried in a name that belongs to nobody, Lucy Martelli. On the twenty-second of July the bank issues him a certificate of deposit for a million and a half dollars, which is afterward split into three of five hundred thousand each.
suggested_refs: Cunningham v. Commissioner of Banks, 249 Mass. 401 (1924), the judicial reconstruction of the Hanover Trust accounts
sources: Cunningham v. Commissioner of Banks, 249 Mass. 401 (1924)

stops.name: Newspaper Row, the admiring front page
stops.date_confidence: attested (Smithsonian). Coordinates corrected to 259-261 Washington Street on Newspaper Row per Boston city directories; an earlier working figure sat about 250 m southwest. Note that Mass Moments, sometimes cited for this, does not in fact mention Grozier or Barron; that page was fetched and checked.
stops.campa: The Boston Post puts him on the front page, the immigrant who turned two dollars and fifty cents into millions, and the story runs warm. Deposits jump the same day. Men mortgage their houses to buy in; policemen and priests and city clerks stand in line with cash in their hands. The paper has done for him what no advertisement could. It takes the editors two days to understand what they have done, and by then Richard Grozier, the acting publisher, is asking a financial journalist named Clarence Barron what a reply coupon is actually worth.
suggested_refs: The Boston Post building, 259-261 Washington Street, Newspaper Row
sources: Pulitzer Prize record, Boston Post, 1921 Public Service

stops.name: 27 School Street, four abreast
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Post turned skeptical on 26 July, that a run followed, and that Ponzi paid out roughly $1-2 million over several days (Smithsonian). The Columbus and Marconi exchange is corrected in context: it belongs here, in the street outside the office at the height of the scheme, not to a late-life interview as commonly retold. The crowd's retort survives in two wordings, 'But you discovered money!' (NEHS, crediting Time) and 'But Charlie, you discovered where the money is!' (Boston Post via Smithsonian); neither is preferred here.
stops.campa: The Post turns skeptical on the twenty-sixth and the crowd on School Street turns with it. The line stands four abreast from the City Hall Annex to his door. Ponzi pays it: a million dollars and more across several days, over the counter to anyone who asks, and the paying calms the street faster than any statement could. He walks out among them in a straw hat and they cheer him. A man in the crowd calls out that he is the greatest Italian of them all.
stops.quote: No, Columbus and Marconi were greater. Columbus discovered America, Marconi discovered the wireless.
stops.quote_source: Ponzi to a supporter in the crowd outside his School Street office, late July 1920, as quoted in New England Historical Society (crediting Time) and reported by the Boston Post via Smithsonian
suggested_refs: Ponzi's own account of the queue in The Rise of Mr. Ponzi: 'A huge line of investors, four abreast, stretched from the City Hall Annex...all the way to my office!'
sources: New England Historical Society, 'Charles Ponzi, The Financial Idiot Who Drove Boston Money Mad in 1920'

stops.name: Newspaper Row, the man he hired
stops.date_confidence: attested (Smithsonian). The exposé ran in the Boston Post on 2 August 1920; the Post pages themselves were not read in facsimile and the account here passes through Smithsonian.
stops.campa: He hires William McMasters, a publicity agent, to handle the press for him, and gives him the run of the office and a retainer. McMasters spends a few days among the papers, working from the firm's own filing cabinets, and concludes that the man employing him is insolvent by millions. He takes what he has found to the Boston Post. On the second of August the paper prints it: the financial genius is a financial incompetent, hopelessly so, and the deficit runs into the millions.
suggested_refs: William McMasters's exposé, Boston Post, 2 August 1920

stops.name: Boston, the involuntary petition
stops.date_confidence: attested; In re Ponzi, 268 F. 997 (D. Mass. 1920). The federal building in which the petition was filed is not identified in the sources reached, so the pin is a downtown Boston placeholder.
stops.campa: Creditors file an involuntary petition in bankruptcy against Ponzi as an individual, not against the Securities Exchange Company, because there is no company to file against: one man, one certificate, one set of pockets. The filing settles the question the whole city has been arguing about all summer, whether there was an enterprise here at all. The answer entered on the docket is no. It has been seven months and fourteen days since he filed the certificate.
suggested_refs: In re Ponzi, 268 F. 997 (D. Mass. 1920), the bankruptcy referee's findings

stops.name: Hanover Trust, the bank taken
stops.date_confidence: attested; Cunningham v. Commissioner of Banks, 249 Mass. 401 (1924), which gives the overdraft as $441,878.07 as of the morning of 10 August 1920 and the seizure on 11 August. Coordinate remains an unconfirmed North End placeholder.
stops.campa: Joseph C. Allen, the Massachusetts bank commissioner, takes possession of Hanover Trust. The court that later untangles the accounts will find the overdraft standing at four hundred forty-one thousand eight hundred seventy-eight dollars and seven cents as of the morning of the tenth of August. Depositors who never heard of the Securities Exchange Company lose their savings because Ponzi bought the stock of their bank. The commissioner's men go through the ledgers looking for Lucy Martelli and cannot find a woman of that name anywhere in Boston.
suggested_refs: Cunningham v. Commissioner of Banks, 249 Mass. 401 (1924)
sources: Cunningham v. Commissioner of Banks, 249 Mass. 401 (1924)

stops.name: Newspaper Row, the wire to Atlanta
stops.date_confidence: attested (Smithsonian; the Pulitzer citation for the Post's series). The 1921 Pulitzer Prize for Public Service is confirmed separately by the Pulitzer record.
stops.campa: The Post, still digging, wires the warden of the federal penitentiary in Atlanta about a prisoner of ten years earlier, and gets back what it needs. On the eleventh it prints the Montreal forgery, the Banco Zarossi years, the alias Bianchi, the whole record he had walked away from on the assumption that nobody in Boston would ever go looking. The paper takes the 1921 Pulitzer Prize for Public Service for the series. Rose learns about her husband's prison years from a newspaper, along with everybody else.
suggested_refs: The Boston Post's 1921 Pulitzer Prize for Public Service, 'for its exposure of the operations of Charles Ponzi'

stops.name: Boston, the surrender and the audit
stops.date_confidence: surrender and mail-fraud charge attested (Smithsonian), which also gives Pride's figure as $3 million 'later revised to $7 million'. The gross-received range of roughly $15 million from 30,000-40,000 people is attested but not reconcilable with the other measures, since principal was reinvested as fast as it was paid. The federal building is a downtown placeholder.
stops.campa: He surrenders to federal authorities and is charged with using the mails to defraud. An auditor named Edwin L. Pride goes into whatever is left of the books and reports him three million dollars in the red, a figure later revised to seven. Between thirty and forty thousand people have handed him money across about eight months, something near fifteen million dollars gross, and nobody can say exactly how much, because the same dollar was paid out and handed back in and counted twice.
stops.quote: My secret is how to cash the coupons. I do not tell it to anyone. Let the United States find it out, if it can.
stops.quote_source: Ponzi, contemporary statement, 1920, as quoted in Mitchell Zuckoff, 'In Ponzi We Trust', Smithsonian Magazine
suggested_refs: Edwin L. Pride's audit of the Securities Exchange Company, 1920

stops.name: Suffolk County Courthouse, twenty-two indictments
stops.date_confidence: attested verbatim in the statement of facts of Ponzi v. Fessenden, 258 U.S. 254 (1922). Pemberton Square was Suffolk County's seat of criminal courts in this period; the specific courthouse building was not separately confirmed by a fetched source.
stops.campa: A Suffolk County grand jury returns twenty-two indictments: eleven counts of larceny, ten of being accessory before the fact, one of conspiracy. The Commonwealth wants him for the money taken from its citizens. The United States wants him for the mails. The two sovereigns will spend the next eighteen months arguing over which of them is entitled to hold his body, and the argument will go all the way up and be decided under his name. He defends himself at the state trials, without counsel.
stops.quote: September 11, 1920, 22 indictments were returned against Charles Ponzi in the superior court for Suffolk county, Mass., charging him with certain larcenies.
stops.quote_source: Ponzi v. Fessenden, 258 U.S. 254 (1922), opinion of the Court (Taft, C.J.), statement of facts
suggested_refs: The Suffolk County criminal courts at Pemberton Square, Boston

stops.name: Plymouth, five years for the mails
stops.date_confidence: date attested verbatim in Ponzi v. Fessenden; some secondary accounts give 1 November and the contradiction is flagged, not resolved, the Court's own statement of facts being preferred. The 1920s Plymouth House of Correction building could not be distinguished from the modern facility on Long Pond Road, so the pin is downtown Plymouth as a placeholder.
stops.campa: He pleads guilty to the first count of one indictment and takes five years in the House of Correction at Plymouth, held there as a federal prisoner. He will serve about three and a half of them. He is thirty-eight years old and has now been inside three prisons in two countries. Which building at Plymouth holds him is not something the sources settle: the 1920 house of correction cannot be told apart from the modern facility on Long Pond Road by anything reachable.
stops.quote: November 30, 1920, he pleaded guilty to the first count of one of these, and was sentenced to imprisonment for five years in the House of Correction at Plymouth, Mass., and committed.
stops.quote_source: Ponzi v. Fessenden, 258 U.S. 254 (1922), opinion of the Court (Taft, C.J.), statement of facts
suggested_refs: The Plymouth House of Correction as it stood in 1920; the building is not distinguishable from its successor in reachable sources

segments.name: Fessenden, the Three Trials, and the Florida Land

stops.name: The Capitol, Washington: Ponzi v. Fessenden
stops.date_confidence: attested; Ponzi v. Fessenden, 258 U.S. 254, decided 27 March 1922. Frequently mis-described as a double-jeopardy case; it is a comity and jurisdiction ruling. Pin note: in 1922 the Supreme Court still sat in the Old Senate Chamber of the Capitol, its own building not opening until 1935, so the stop is pinned at the Capitol.
stops.campa: The Supreme Court takes up the question of who owns his body. Massachusetts wants him produced for trial while he is serving a federal sentence, and he argues that being handed back and forth between two sovereigns is not a thing the Constitution allows to be done to a man. Chief Justice Taft writes for the Court that a federal prisoner may be lent to a state with federal consent and returned afterward, the two governments being neighbours rather than rivals. The Court is sitting in the old Senate chamber; it has no building of its own until 1935.
suggested_refs: Ponzi v. Fessenden, 258 U.S. 254 (1922), still cited on federal-state comity in the custody of prisoners
sources: Ponzi v. Fessenden, 258 U.S. 254 (1922), text via FindLaw

stops.name: Suffolk County Courthouse, a common and notorious thief
stops.date_confidence: attested; first trial October 1924 ending in acquittal on the first ten larceny counts, second hung, third in February 1925 producing the verdict and the seven-to-nine-year sentence, affirmed in Commonwealth v. Ponzi, 256 Mass. 159 (1926). Corrects an earlier blurred dating of the third trial to 1927, which is the year he began serving. The $14,000 appellate bail is distinct from the $1,500 Florida bond.
stops.campa: The Commonwealth tries him three times. At the first, in October 1924, he defends himself and is acquitted on the first ten larceny counts. The second jury hangs. The third convicts, and the court adjudges him a common and notorious thief, which is a formal status under Massachusetts law and carries seven to nine years. He is let out on fourteen thousand dollars bail while the appeal runs. Where the fourteen thousand comes from, for a man just adjudged a thief, no source reached says. He does not spend the interval in Boston.
suggested_refs: Commonwealth v. Ponzi, 256 Mass. 159, 152 N.E. 307 (1926), affirming the conviction and the 'common and notorious thief' adjudication
sources: American Heritage, 'Bubble, Bubble No, Toil, No Trouble' (February 1973)

stops.name: Springfield, Jacksonville: Charles Borelli takes rooms
stops.date_confidence: date, alias and block attested by The Jaxson, 'Jacksonville's Notorious Con Artist: Charles Ponzi' (fetched); corroborated in outline by Wikipedia's Florida section.
stops.campa: He arrives in Jacksonville with Rose on the twenty-eighth of September under the name Charles Borelli, and takes rooms in the Springfield neighbourhood on the 1300 block of Main Street. Florida is in the last months of its land boom, when a lot changes hands three times in a week and nobody walks the ground. He has been in this state before, painting signs he could not paint. He is forty-three now, with a Massachusetts conviction on appeal behind him and another man's name on the rooming-house register.
suggested_refs: The Springfield neighbourhood of Jacksonville, 1300 block of Main Street
sources: The Jaxson, Ennis Davis and Kelsi Hasden, 'Jacksonville's Notorious Con Artist: Charles Ponzi' (2018)

stops.name: Columbia County, the tracts named for his family
stops.date_confidence: the syndicate, the acreage, the price, the lot size, the tract names and the first sale date are attested by The Jaxson (fetched). Coordinates are approximate, centred near Lake City about 65 miles west of Jacksonville; the exact parcel was not pinpointed.
stops.campa: About a hundred acres near Lake City are bought at roughly sixteen dollars the acre, part of it swamp, and cut into lots the size of a room. The Charpon Land Syndicate, being Ponzi, Rose, and Mr. and Mrs. Calcadonio Alviati, sells them at ten dollars each with two hundred percent promised inside sixty days. The tracts are named Rosa Maria for his wife, Oreste for his father, Imelde for his mother. The first sale goes through on the ninth of November. About seven thousand dollars comes in before the state stops it.
suggested_refs: The Charpon Land Syndicate tracts in Columbia County, Florida, named Rosa Maria, Oreste and Imelde
sources: The Jaxson, 'Jacksonville's Notorious Con Artist: Charles Ponzi' (2018)

stops.name: Duval County Courthouse, a year at hard labour
stops.date_confidence: indictment and sentence attested (The Jaxson; Wikipedia's Florida section). Building corrected: the courthouse in use in 1926 was the third Duval County Courthouse, built 1902 by Rutledge Holmes at 330 East Bay Street; an earlier working coordinate sat several hundred metres south toward the river, and the 2012 courthouse on West Adams Street is irrelevant to 1926.
stops.campa: A Duval County grand jury indicts him for violating Florida's trust and securities law, and on the twenty-sixth of April the court gives him a year at hard labour at Raiford. He posts fifteen hundred dollars and walks out on appeal. That makes two appeals running at once in two states and two sets of bail money out on him, and one man in the middle of it who has worked out that the interval between conviction and prison is a country a person can live in. The courthouse is the 1902 building on East Bay Street, four blocks up from the river.
suggested_refs: The third Duval County Courthouse (1902, Rutledge Holmes), 330 East Bay Street, Jacksonville
sources: The Jaxson, 'Jacksonville's Notorious Con Artist: Charles Ponzi' (2018)

stops.name: Tampa, the shaved head
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the staged suicide, the disguise, the alias and the freighter (The Jaxson). Exact Tampa location, dock or neighbourhood, is not specified in the source, so city-centre coordinates are used; the day within June is not established.
stops.campa: He leaves his clothes on a beach with an apologetic note, so that the state will spend its time looking for a body, and goes to Tampa. There he shaves his head, grows a moustache, and signs onto an Italian freighter as a waiter under the name Andrea Luciana. He is forty-four and waiting tables again, which is the work he did in New York at twenty-two. The ship is the Sic Vos Non Vobis, bound out of American waters. The Latin on her is from a line said to be Virgil's about bees: thus you labour, but not for yourselves.
suggested_refs: The Italian freighter Sic Vos Non Vobis, on which Ponzi shipped as a waiter under the name Andrea Luciana
sources: The Jaxson, 'Jacksonville's Notorious Con Artist: Charles Ponzi' (2018)

stops.name: Port of New Orleans, taken off the freighter
stops.date_confidence: arrest aboard the Sic Vos Non Vobis at New Orleans, before the ship cleared U.S. jurisdiction, is attested (The Jaxson). Wharf and berth are not specified; general riverfront coordinates used. That he appealed to Coolidge and to Mussolini is documented; the widely repeated joke that the two leaders agreed on nothing except refusing him is later journalistic folklore and is not in any record reached.
stops.campa: Federal agents take him off the freighter at her New Orleans call, before she clears United States jurisdiction, and the alias is finished. From the cell he writes to President Coolidge asking to be deported instead of imprisoned, and then, getting nothing, to Mussolini in Rome, asking Italy to claim one of its own. Neither answers. Thirteen years later he will be drawing a wage in Brazil from an airline the Italian state owns, put there by Mussolini's own pilot.
suggested_refs: Ponzi's 1926 appeals to Calvin Coolidge and to Benito Mussolini for deportation in lieu of imprisonment
sources: The Jaxson, 'Jacksonville's Notorious Con Artist: Charles Ponzi' (2018)

stops.name: Boston, the seven to nine years begin
stops.date_confidence: attested that he began the Massachusetts term in February 1927 at Charlestown State Prison after Commonwealth v. Ponzi affirmed (American Heritage, February 1973). Pin note, stated openly: no coordinate for Charlestown State Prison is established by any source in this research pool, so the stop is pinned at the Suffolk County courthouse from which the sentence issued rather than at an invented location.
stops.campa: The appeal fails. Commonwealth v. Ponzi is affirmed, and in February he begins the seven to nine years at Charlestown, the state prison across the river, having already served federal time at Plymouth for the mails and dodged a Florida year at hard labour by going to sea. Charlestown makes the fourth prison of his life, after Saint-Vincent-de-Paul, Atlanta and Plymouth. He is forty-four. He will be inside for seven years, and comes out in 1934, into a country that has been in a depression since the autumn of 1929.
suggested_refs: Charlestown State Prison, Boston, where the 1925 sentence was served from February 1927; its coordinates are not established in this pool
sources: American Heritage, 'Bubble, Bubble No, Toil, No Trouble' (February 1973)

stops.name: Massachusetts State House, the pardon refused
stops.date_confidence: that Governor Joseph B. Ely denied the pardon and the relief from deportation in July 1934 is attested; that the denial issued from the State House itself rather than from another executive office is inferred and is flagged here as unconfirmed placement.
stops.campa: Released, he asks Governor Joseph B. Ely for a pardon and for relief from deportation, on the ground that he has a wife in this state and thirty-one years of his life in this country. Ely refuses. Ponzi never took citizenship: seventeen years in the United States before the scheme, and never a paper filed, so the law is free to put him on a boat, and does. Whether the petition was denied in this building or in some other office is not recorded anywhere reached.
suggested_refs: Governor Joseph B. Ely's July 1934 denial of pardon and of relief from deportation

stops.name: Boston Harbor, the Vulcania
stops.date_confidence: date attested; the ship and port are documented, not inferred. The U.S. Immigration Service put Ponzi aboard the SS Vulcania in Boston Harbor for a single passage to Italy, per a contemporary press photograph held by UMBC Special Collections and captioned '[Charles Ponzi is deported on board the S.S. Vulcania to Italy.]'
stops.campa: The Immigration Service walks him up the gangway of the SS Vulcania in Boston Harbor and buys him one passage to Italy. A press photographer catches him on deck with his hat on, fifty-two years old, deported as an undesirable alien. He came into this harbour thirty-one years ago on the Vancouver out of Naples with nothing, and he leaves it on a ship somebody else has chosen for him, with nothing. He has been in the country thirty-one years and has spent more than twelve of them in prison. Rose stays in Boston and goes back to work.
suggested_refs: UMBC Special Collections press photograph, '[Charles Ponzi is deported on board the S.S. Vulcania to Italy.]'
sources: UMBC Special Collections, press photograph caption

stops.name: Rome, the book the printer would not release
stops.date_confidence: the printing history is attested (thefirstedition.com): printed by the Pacific Printing Company in 1937 under Ponzi's own imprint, the first 1,000 copies withheld against an unpaid bill of $235, released in 1938. The commonly cited date of 1936 appears to be the cover date of the 2001 Inkwell Publishers reprint and is flagged as such. Details of Ponzi's Italian years generally are sparse and derive heavily from his own self-report.
stops.campa: He writes his life and calls it The Rise of Mr. Ponzi, and the Pacific Printing Company sets it and prints it. Then the printer holds the first thousand copies against an unpaid bill of two hundred and thirty-five dollars, and the author of the largest fraud in living American memory cannot raise two hundred and thirty-five dollars. He appeals in the press for a backer. Somebody eventually pays it and the book comes out in 1938. The sequel he plans, to be called The Fall of Mr. Ponzi, is never written.
stops.quote: I haven't got a cent... I'm sure there must be someone in the United States who would be willing to pay the bill for me.
stops.quote_source: Ponzi's public appeal for a backer to release the withheld first printing, quoted in thefirstedition.com's catalogue entry for The Rise of Mr. Ponzi
suggested_refs: The Rise of Mr. Ponzi, Pacific Printing Company, printed 1937, released 1938; the unwritten sequel The Fall of Mr. Ponzi
sources: thefirstedition.com, catalogue entry for The Rise of Mr. Ponzi

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the airline desk
stops.date_confidence: the post, the route and Biseo are attested (Wikipedia; Italian aviation histories): Attilio Biseo, reported second cousin, LATI director from 1939 and Mussolini's personal pilot. Placement is reconstruction: no Rio office address exists in any source located and the coordinate is a bare city centroid. Claims of direct personal appointment by Mussolini are unverified, and currency-smuggling allegations attached to this period are allegation, not conviction.
stops.campa: A second cousin, the aviator Attilio Biseo, who flies Mussolini personally and directs the new transatlantic line, finds him a commercial post in Brazil. LATI runs Rome to Seville to Ilha do Sal to Recife to Rio, the South Atlantic taken in stages, carrying mail and passengers and, the Allies are certain, other things besides. Ponzi is fifty-seven and drawing a wage from a state airline on a continent he has never seen. In December 1941 LATI stops flying the route, and he is out of work at fifty-nine.
suggested_refs: LATI, Linee Aeree Transcontinentali Italiane, and the Rome-Seville-Ilha do Sal-Recife-Rio route, 1939 to December 1941

stops.name: Hospital Sao Francisco de Assis, the charity ward
stops.date_confidence: death date, hospital, charity ward and the roughly $75 estate are attested (Wikipedia; Smithsonian). The eyesight detail is corrected: Wikipedia gives blind in one eye, not nearly blind. Continuity between the 1949 charity hospital and today's UFRJ teaching hospital of the same name on Avenida Presidente Vargas was not independently documented, so the coordinate is held at moderate confidence. Neither source names the AP reporter or dates the dispatch.
stops.campa: A stroke in the early months of 1948 takes part of his movement and the sight of one eye. He lives on the charity of friends, among them a barber named Francisco Nonato Nunes, and dies on the eighteenth of January in the charity ward of the Hospital Sao Francisco de Assis, sixty-six years old, with about seventy-five dollars to his name. Months before the end an Associated Press reporter sits down by the bed and gets the plainest account of the business anyone ever gets out of him.
stops.quote: Those were confused, money-mad days. Everybody wanted to make a killing... My business was simple. It was the old game of robbing Peter to pay Paul.
stops.quote_source: Ponzi to an Associated Press reporter, hospital-bed interview months before his death, as quoted in TIME, Olivia B. Waxman, 19 May 2017
suggested_refs: Hospital Sao Francisco de Assis, Cidade Nova, Rio de Janeiro, and its charity ward
sources: TIME, Olivia B. Waxman, 'What to Know About the Original Ponzi Scheme' (19 May 2017)

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the grave with no marker
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; burial in an unmarked paupers' grave in Rio is reported by NNDB, a tertiary database, used here because no primary cemetery register was located. Caju Cemetery history pages and Find a Grave could not confirm cemetery name or plot, so none is named. The date is the day after death, an ordering placeholder. The last reported remark about the show survives only through journalistic transmission and its exact wording is uncertain.
stops.campa: He is buried in Rio among the indigent, in a grave with no marker on it. No register naming him has been found, no plot number, no stone. In Lugo, where he was born, there is nothing either: a traveller who goes looking finds the Rocca Estense and no sign that the town has ever claimed him. What survives is the word. American federal regulators still use his surname as the technical term for paying old investors out of new investors' money, an arrangement he neither invented nor named.
stops.quote: Even if they never got anything for it, it was cheap at that price. Without malice aforethought I had given them the best show that was ever staged in their territory since the landing of the Pilgrims! It was easily worth fifteen million bucks to watch me put the thing over.
stops.quote_source: Ponzi's last interview near the end of his life, as quoted in Mitchell Zuckoff, 'In Ponzi We Trust', Smithsonian Magazine, and in New England Historical Society; wording varies between retellings and no interviewer, publication or date is named in either
suggested_refs: The unlocated paupers' grave in Rio de Janeiro
Investor.gov and the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission's standing definition of a 'Ponzi scheme'
sources: wanderingitaly.com, 'Pilgrimage and Ponzi Schemes: Lugo, Italy'
